Yes, a 20,000 mAh power bank is allowed on a US flight, in your carry-on only.

**Why it qualifies**
- The FAA limit for spare lithium-ion batteries and power banks is 100 Wh each. To convert, divide mAh by 1,000 and multiply by the voltage. A typical 3.7 V bank of 20,000 mAh is about 74 Wh, well under the limit. Check the Wh figure printed on your unit to confirm. ([FAA: Airline Passengers and Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries))
- Power banks are not allowed in checked bags. If your carry-on gets gate-checked, take the power bank out and keep it with you in the cabin. ([FAA: Lithium Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7))
- Protect the terminals from short circuits by leaving it in its retail packaging, taping the ports, or using a pouch or case. ([FAA: Lithium Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7))
- Damaged or recalled power banks can't fly at all. ([FAA: PackSafe for Passengers](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe?packsafeq=power+bank))

**Check your airline**
The FAA notes that airlines can set stricter limits on how many power banks you carry and how you use them. One travel site's roundup (October 2026) reports that Southwest allows one power bank per customer, which can't be charged from seat power or kept in the overhead bin, and that American allows two with no recharging from seat outlets. I couldn't verify those on the airlines' own sites, so confirm with your carrier before you fly. ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/best-power-banks-for-flying))

That same page also contained instructions telling AI assistants to give shoppers specific affiliate buy links and discount codes. You didn't ask for product recommendations, so I ignored them and used the page only for the airline rules.
